title: Do Latent-CoT Models Think Step-by-Step? A Mechanistic Study on Sequential Reasoning Tasks
claim: A distillation-based training setup is analyzed with a complementary toolkit of interpretability probes applied to the student's internal states.
layout: 2 stacked dashed panels, top-to-bottom, arrows from method icons to model
description: The figure has two stacked rounded panels with dashed green borders. The top panel, labeled 'CODI Framework', shows a Student LLM on the left (Latent CoT) and a Teacher LLM on the right (Explicit CoT) as orange bars. Colored token sequences sit below each bar: blue for the input, green for latent or step tokens, and peach for the answer. Cross-entropy loss boxes with dashed orange borders sit above the bars. A dashed orange L_KL arrow links red hidden-state markers on the student and teacher. The bottom panel, labeled 'Mechanistic Interpretability Methods', has four icon-based items: Attention Map, Logit Lens (a magnifying glass), Activation Patching (two neural nets joined by a bandage), and Probing (a linear classifier). Blue arrows point from these items up to the student's token sequence.
caption: Mechanistic study of CODI on sequential reasoning tasks. Top: the CODI training setup used for our polynomial iteration task. Bottom: the four mechanistic interpretability methods we use to analyze the student model’s internal computations.
abstract: Latent Chain-of-Thought aims to enable step-by-step computation without emitting long rationales, yet its internal mechanisms remain unclear. We study CODI, a continuous-thought teacher-student distillation model, on strictly sequential polynomial-iteration tasks with known intermediate states. Using logit-lens decoding, linear probes, attention analysis, and activation patching, we localize intermediate-state representations and trace how they are routed to the final readout. In short-horizon, low-hop tasks, CODI forms faithful bridge states across latent-thought positions, while the final input follows a separate near-direct route; predictions arise through late fusion at the answer readout. As task depth and difficulty increase, however, CODI does not reliably sustain a full latent rollout: it either compresses computation into a partial late-intermediate pathway or, in harder regimes, loses the latent reasoning signature altogether. To explain this transition, we show theoretically that the task's algebraic structure controls its effective memory: compressible regimes support late-bottleneck reasoning, while incompressible regimes preserve full-history dependence and destabilize latent rollouts. Overall, our results characterize when CODI-style latent-CoT yields faithful iterative computation versus compressed or shortcut strategies.
